title: Kurma Avataram
body:
Kurma Avataram

There was once a celestial dancer who wished to please Goddess Maha Lakshmi, and danced with such elegance and devotion that the Goddess appeared before her and blessed her with a divine garland, fragrant beyond compare — so fragrant that swarms of bees followed wherever it went. As the dancer left, the sage Durvasa passed by, and when she offered him the garland he accepted it graciously. But the ceaseless buzzing of the bees soon irritated him, and seeking to be rid of the garland he came upon Indra seated atop his elephant Airavata. Durvasa presented it to Indra, who in his pride placed it carelessly upon Airavata's head; the elephant, overwhelmed by its scent, flung it down and trampled it underfoot. Enraged by this contempt for a gift born of the Goddess's grace, Durvasa cursed Indra that he and all the world would lose their wealth.
Because the curse was worded loosely, its effect was sweeping. The greatest wealth of all is Maha Lakshmi herself, and bound by the curse she disappeared from the heavens; with her went the Kalpavriksha, the wish-fulfilling tree, and Kamadhenu, the celestial cow, and all abundance besides. For the first time Indra, who had never known lack, found himself helpless. He hurried to Vaikuntham and fell at the feet of Sriman Narayana, who told him that wealth is not something owned but something earned, and that to reclaim what was lost he must churn the ocean of milk, in whose depths lay all that had vanished, Maha Lakshmi among them.
Indra accepted the task, but knew the Devas alone lacked the strength for it, and so approached the Danavas with an offer: aid in the churning, and share in whatever treasures emerged. Tempted by the promise of riches, they agreed. Mount Mandara was made the churning rod and Vasuki, king of serpents, the churning rope. But as the churning began the mountain sank into the ocean, and no effort of Devas or Danavas could keep it afloat. Then Sriman Narayana took the form of Kurma, the great tortoise, and descending into the depths bore Mount Mandara upon His back, holding it steady so that the churning could go on. Even so the mountain wavered atop the tossing waters, and the Lord in another form pressed down upon its summit from above, so that it was held firm both from below and above as the great work continued.
One by one the ocean yielded its treasures. The first to rise was the deadly poison Halahala, which threatened all creation until Shiva, out of compassion, drank it and held it in His throat, which turned blue from its potency. Then came, in no fixed order, the celestial horse Uchaishravas, the Kalpavriksha, Kamadhenu, and Chandra the moon; and at last Maha Lakshmi herself emerged, and prosperity returned to the worlds. Indra bowed before her seeking forgiveness, and she reclaimed her place in Vaikuntham beside the Lord. The final treasure to rise was Dhanvantari, the celestial physician and an incarnation of the Lord, bearing a golden chalice of Amrutham, the nectar of immortality.
Both Devas and Danavas rushed to claim the nectar, and a battle seemed certain, until the Lord took the enchanting form of Mohini. Beguiled by her beauty, the Danavas allowed her to distribute the nectar, but she poured it only into the cups of the Devas. One among the Danavas, Rahu, saw through the illusion and, disguising himself as a Deva, sat among them and drank; but before the nectar could pass his throat, Surya and Chandra recognized him and alerted the Lord. At once Sriman Narayana released His Sudarshana Chakra and severed Rahu's body in two. Because a drop of the nectar had already reached him, he did not die. Seeing a serpent slither past, the Lord cut it likewise in two, and joined the serpent's tail to Rahu's upper half and its hood to his lower half — and so were formed the two beings Rahu and Ketu. With the nectar consumed, the Devas regained their strength and Indra's rule was restored. Yet the deeper lesson of the churning endured: that all wealth, all power, all status is meaningless without the grace of Sriman Narayana, for even the mightiest Devas cannot act without His will.
